content: Lymphatic filariasis is a parasitic disease caused by microscopic, thread-like worms. These adult worms reside exclusively in the human lymphatic system, which is responsible for maintaining the body's fluid balance and defending against infections. The disease is transmitted from one person to another through mosquito bites. Individuals affected by lymphatic filariasis may develop lymphedema, elephantiasis, or, in men, a condition known as hydrocele, which involves swelling of the scrotum. This disease is a significant cause of permanent disability worldwide. Those disfigured by the condition often face social stigma and rejection, and their inability to work due to disability negatively impacts their families and communities. Lymphatic filariasis has been affecting humans for thousands of years, with evidence suggesting its presence as far back as 1500–4000 years ago. The first documented description of its symptoms dates to the 16th century, when Jan Huygen Linschoten observed the disease during his exploration of Goa. The disease begins when infective larvae are transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected mosquito during a blood meal. These larvae migrate to the lymphatic vessels and lymph nodes, where they mature into adult worms capable of producing microfilariae. The adult worms can live in the lymphatic system for several years. Female worms release microfilariae into the bloodstream, which can then be ingested by mosquitoes during subsequent bites. Inside the mosquito, the microfilariae develop into infective third-stage larvae over 1 to 2 weeks. When the mosquito bites another human, these larvae are transmitted to the new host, continuing the cycle. The causative agents of lymphatic filariasis are nematodes, or roundworms, that inhabit the lymphatic vessels and nodes of the human host. The primary species responsible for the disease are Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, and Brugia timori. The risk of acquiring lymphatic filariasis increases with repeated mosquito bites over months or years. Individuals who live in tropical or subtropical regions where the disease is endemic are at the highest risk. Short-term travelers to these areas, however, have a very low risk of infection. Most individuals infected with lymphatic filariasis remain asymptomatic and never develop clinical symptoms, even though the parasite causes damage to the lymphatic system. A small percentage of infected individuals may develop lymphedema, and in some cases, filarial infection can lead to pulmonary tropical eosinophilia syndrome. These clinical manifestations often appear years after the initial infection. For diagnosis, serologic techniques are an alternative to microscopic detection of microfilariae. Patients with active filarial infections typically exhibit elevated levels of antifilarial IgG4 in their blood, which can be detected using routine assays. The immunochromatographic card test (ICT), which is highly sensitive and specific for detecting Wuchereria bancrofti infection, has simplified the diagnostic process. This test requires only 100 μl of fingerprick blood and can be performed at any time of day. Treatment for lymphatic filariasis involves the use of diethylcarbamazine (DEC), a medication taken annually that kills the microfilariae circulating in the blood. While DEC does not eliminate all adult worms, it prevents infected individuals from transmitting the disease to others. However, DEC is not indicated for treating lymphedema or elephantiasis, as these conditions are typically not associated with active filarial infections. Physicians can obtain DEC from the CDC after laboratory confirmation of infection. Periodic blood examinations to detect infection and timely initiation of treatment can also help prevent the development of clinical symptoms.
